title: House prices in tourist hotspots increasingly out of reach for young and low paid
meta_description: Rising house prices and private rents mean that some workers are at risk of being priced out of living in rural and coastal areas, contributing to skill shortages in the tourism and hospitality industries that their local economies rely on.

breadcrumb.text: House prices in tourist hotspots increasingly out of reach for young and low paid

lede: Rising house prices and private rents mean that some workers are at risk of being priced out of living in rural and coastal areas, contributing to skill shortages in the tourism and hospitality industries that their local economies rely on.

body.text: 28 September 2021
Young and low paid workers in tourist hotspots are increasingly facing the prospect of being unable to afford to live there.

Despite falling from a record high in June, the [average UK house price (£256,000) increased by 8.0% in July 2021](https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/inflationandpriceindices/bulletins/housepriceindex/july2021) compared with the previous year.

House prices were rising at three times the national rate in some rural and coastal areas in July, such as Conwy in North Wales (25.0%), North Devon (22.5%) and Richmondshire in the Yorkshire Dales (21.4%), continuing a trend seen during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.
Meanwhile, the seven areas that recorded house price falls in July were all London boroughs.

House prices are increasing partly because of temporary changes to taxes paid on property purchases (including [Stamp Duty in England and Northern Ireland](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/stamp-duty-land-tax-temporary-reduced-rates)), but they also reflect a shift in consumer preferences with growth being driven by rural and coastal areas.
Prospective home buyers are seeking more space, with prices for detached houses (9.0% growth in July) consistently rising faster than terraced houses (7.7%) or flats (6.1%).

As a result, people living in rural and coastal areas – particularly the young and those on lower incomes – are [at risk of being priced out](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bbcthree/article/dd1d3768-0450-4b07-99e4-fee8e9fd9895) of the housing market.

This could be contributing to [hospitality businesses being unable to fill vacancies](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/employmentandemployeetypes/articles/hospitalitybusinessesaremostlikelytobestrugglingtofillvacancies/2021-09-16), with the industry being predominant in tourist areas and containing a high proportion of young and low paid workers.

body.h2: Growth of tenant demand appears to be exceeding supply
body.text: Growth of tenant demand appears to be exceeding supply

body.h2: Growth of tenant demand appears to be exceeding supply
body.text: UK private rents [increased by 1.3% in the 12 months to August](https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/inflationandpriceindices/bulletins/indexofprivatehousingrentalprices/august2021), rising to 2.0% excluding London.

body.h2: Growth of tenant demand appears to be exceeding supply
body.text: The fastest rates of growth were in the East Midlands (2.7%) and the South West (2.6%), while London was the only region to record a decrease (-0.4%).

body.h2: Growth of tenant demand appears to be exceeding supply
body.text: The [RICS UK Residential Market Survey (PDF, 4.8MB)](https://www.rics.org/globalassets/rics-website/media/news/press-releases/final---8._web_-august_2021_rics_uk_residential_market_survey_tp.pdf) suggests that an imbalance between tenant demand and the supply of lettings could be contributing to the increase in rental prices.

body.h2: Growth of tenant demand appears to be exceeding supply
body.text: In the three months to August 2021, RICS reported that tenant demand was accelerating while landlord instructions remained in decline.

body.h2: Growth of tenant demand appears to be exceeding supply
body.text: The fall in supply of lettings was most widespread in the Midlands, the East of England and the South West.

body.h2: Growth of tenant demand appears to be exceeding supply
body.text: It could be that some landlords are trying to capitalise on domestic tourism through holiday lets, leaving fewer long-term lets for prospective tenants.

body.h2: Growth of tenant demand appears to be exceeding supply
body.text: This is a particular issue for those looking to rent in tourist hotspots, where rates of second home ownership are much higher than average. [Research suggests that many second homes have become holiday lets during the pandemic](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-58460350).

body.h2: People who work in tourist hotspots are generally low paid
body.text: People who work in tourist hotspots are generally low paid

body.h2: People who work in tourist hotspots are generally low paid
body.text: Those who work in tourist hotspots earn less on average than people who live there.

body.h2: People who work in tourist hotspots are generally low paid
body.text: For example, as of April 2020, Cotswold residents earned 28.7% more than people who were employed in the area. There were similar differences between the earnings of residents and workers in other tourist areas such as Derbyshire Dales (27.5%) and Allerdale (24.5%).

body.h2: People who work in tourist hotspots are generally low paid
body.text: This is comparable with areas of Outer London such as Bexley (29.0%) and Harrow (27.3%) that are subject to the “commuter effect”, where people who earn high incomes in the city centre live on the outskirts.

body.h2: People who work in tourist hotspots are generally low paid
body.text: In tourist hotspots, workers earn less than residents because of the types of jobs in those areas, with hospitality being the largest employer.

body.h2: People who work in tourist hotspots are generally low paid
body.text: The median hospitality salary for a full-time employee was £22,779 per year in April 2020, which was 28% lower than the national average of £31,461.

body.h2: People who work in tourist hotspots are generally low paid
body.text: [Hospitality workers were also the most likely to be furloughed during the pandemic](https://www.ons.gov.uk/businessindustryandtrade/business/businessservices/articles/comparisonoffurloughedjobsdata/march2020tojune2021#comparisons-between-bics-estimates-and-cjrs-statistics). On average, between 23 March 2020 and 31 July 2021, more than half of employees in hospitality were furloughed.

body.h2: People who work in tourist hotspots are generally low paid
body.text: As a result, tourist hotspots were among the areas with the highest average furlough rates during the pandemic.

body.h2: People who work in tourist hotspots are generally low paid
body.text: South Lakeland and Eden in the Lake District recorded the highest monthly furlough rates of anywhere in the country, at 40% and 39% respectively in June 2020.

body.h2: Young and low paid at greatest risk of being priced out
body.text: Young and low paid at greatest risk of being priced out

body.h2: Young and low paid at greatest risk of being priced out
body.text: While house prices have been rising during the pandemic, many people have seen their income fall because of furlough, reduced hours or losing their job.

body.h2: Young and low paid at greatest risk of being priced out
body.text: The poorest fifth of workers were more likely than the richest fifth to see a drop in income in the 12 months to March 2021 (42% compared with 31%), according to [recent analysis](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/personalandhouseholdfinances/expenditure/articles/weeklyhouseholdspendingfellbymorethan100onaverageduringthecoronaviruspandemic/2021-09-13).

body.h2: Young and low paid at greatest risk of being priced out
body.text: [Data from the Opinions and Lifestyle Survey (OPN)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/wellbeing/datasets/agegroupsplitestimatesonpersonalandeconomicwellbeingacrosstime) show that young people (aged under 30) have been more likely to report reduced income than those aged over 60, but less likely to do so than 30- to 59-year-olds.

body.h2: Young and low paid at greatest risk of being priced out
body.text: However, young people remain worse off than other age groups in terms of their overall financial situation. A third (34%) of under 30s responding to the [Survey on Living Conditions (SLC)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/personalandhouseholdfinances/incomeandwealth/datasets/economicwellbeingestimatesfromthesurveyoflivingconditionsgreatbritain) had at least some difficulty making ends meet in the year to March 2021, the highest percentage of any age group.

body.h2: Young and low paid at greatest risk of being priced out
body.text: This has implications for the industries that tourism economies rely on, such as hospitality which is reporting record levels of job vacancies.

body.h2: Young and low paid at greatest risk of being priced out
body.text: Nearly a third of hospitality businesses were finding vacancies difficult to fill in late August 2021 (30%), amid [reports of workers being priced out of buying or renting near their job](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-57403083).

body.h2: Young and low paid at greatest risk of being priced out
body.text: We do not yet know the full impact of coronavirus on housing affordability. The [most recent data cover April 2020](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/housing/bulletins/housingaffordabilityinenglandandwales/2020), towards the beginning of the pandemic and before the subsequent rise in house prices.

body.h2: Young and low paid at greatest risk of being priced out
body.text: The next housing affordability release (with data up to April 2021) is due to be published in spring 2022.

body.h2: Young and low paid at greatest risk of being priced out
body.text: There is further analysis of [house price trends before and during the pandemic](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/understandingtownsinenglandandwaleshousepriceanalysis) planned for October 2021.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Measuring the data

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: In this article, we define tourist hotspots as the local authorities with the highest number of travel and tourism businesses per resident population.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Using a [list of travel and tourism industries](https://www.ons.gov.uk/businessindustryandtrade/tourismindustry/articles/coronavirusandtheimpactontheuktravelandtourismindustry/2021-02-15#list-of-industries-used-in-this-analysis), we found the average number of travel and tourism businesses (local units) in each local authority in the years 2017, 2018 and 2019, from the Inter-Departmental Business Register (IDBR).

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: We then divided the resident population of each local authority by the number of travel and tourism businesses to identify tourist hotspots.
